forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
intro: Two people walk through a cold wood; the woman tells her companion she is carrying another man’s child. The Hollywood String Quartet and two guests play the original six-string Verklärte Nacht, with the LP’s first side ending just before his answer.

sections.label: A · Low strings in the wood
sections.mNote: A descending phrase above repeated low notes

sections.label: B · The woman’s confession continues
sections.mNote: Six strings carry the woman’s troubled account

sections.label: C · A violin melody in E major
sections.mNote: Long violin phrases above moving viola and cello parts

sections.label: D · The walk after the confession
sections.mNote: The woman waits for her companion’s answer

sections.label: Link · E♭ minor leaves a low B♭
sections.mNote: The second cello holds the link to side two

cues.title: Footsteps in the low strings
cues.text: A second viola and second cello repeat low D. Above them, the first viola and first cello begin a descending phrase, marked immer leise — always quiet. The violins wait before joining the walk.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score, Dreililien-Verlag, plate 345 (1905), p. 3, bars 1–9, composer’s copy at the Arnold Schönberg Center. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A child, another man
cues.text: Richard Dehmel’s poem puts two people beneath bare trees and a bright moon. “Ich trag ein Kind, und nit von Dir” — “I carry a child, and it is not yours.” The woman speaks; her companion has yet to answer.
cues.evidence: Dehmel, Verklärte Nacht, Weib und Welt (1896), reproduced on p. 2 of the sextet score (Dreililien-Verlag, 1905). Translation ours. https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/manuskripte.php?werke_id=420&id_quelle=1213&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: September in Payerbach
cues.text: In September 1899 Schoenberg spends a holiday in Payerbach with Alexander Zemlinsky and his sister Mathilde. He composes Verklärte Nacht in three weeks. Mathilde will become his wife; the finished manuscript bears the date 1 December.
cues.evidence: Therese Muxeneder, Arnold Schönberg Center work essay: Payerbach holiday, three-week composition and final manuscript date. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: A poem for six strings
cues.text: In 1902 Schoenberg explains his ambition: to bring the poetic storytelling of orchestral music into chamber music. Dehmel’s speakers have no singer here. Two violins, two violas and two cellos tell the whole story.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s announcement in Deutsche Tonkünstler-Zeitung, 21 October 1902, reproduced by the Arnold Schönberg Center. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: The violin in E major
cues.text: E major opens a gentler passage. The first violin stretches its melody over moving figures in the second viola and first cello. Etwas ruhiger, Schoenberg writes: a little calmer. In his account of the poem, this theme belongs to the woman’s longing for motherhood.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 12–13; Schoenberg’s programme notes (1950), fourth theme, example 7. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: She waits for his answer
cues.text: The woman’s confession is over. In Dehmel’s poem she walks awkwardly beside the man she loves and looks up at the moon. His reply begins by lifting the burden from her unborn child.
cues.evidence: Dehmel, Verklärte Nacht (1896), third and fourth stanzas, reproduced in the original sextet score, p. 2; Schoenberg’s 1950 commentary places this scene before the D-major answer. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: One low B♭ remains
cues.text: The strings settle into E♭ minor and withdraw until a low B♭ remains in the second cello. The LP side ends with that note still awaiting its answer. Side two opens in D major.
cues.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 24–26, bars 204–229; Schoenberg’s 1950 commentary explains the E♭-minor ending and its connecting B♭. The LP division is at bars 228–229. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A violin melody in E major
transitions.to: C · A violin melody in E major
transitions.how: The sextet broadens, marked Breiter, then enters the gentler E-major episode. At Etwas ruhiger, the first violin carries the long melody while the second viola and first cello keep moving beneath it; the second cello supplies the slower bass.
transitions.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 12–13, and Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, example 7. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

transitions.title: The second cello keeps B♭
transitions.from: D · The walk after the confession
transitions.to: Link · E♭ minor leaves a low B♭
transitions.how: The upper strings taper away over E♭ minor. The second cello keeps B♭ after the other parts have stopped; that surviving bass note connects the first half to the broad D-major answer on the next side.
transitions.evidence: Dreililien sextet score (1905), pp. 24–26, bars 204–229; Schoenberg’s 1950 programme notes, examples 9–10. https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

source.title: Schoenberg, Verklärte Nacht, original sextet score, Dreililien-Verlag, plate 345 (1905), composer’s copy E1
source.locator: Pages 3, 12–13 and 24–25, bars 1–228. Two violins, two violas and two cellos; the two viola parts and the two cello parts are grouped together here.

timeline.note: First viola and first cello descend over the low D repeated by their partners.
Both violins join the descending phrases of the violas and cellos.
All six strings play, passing melodic phrases between the upper and lower instruments.
The first violin sings in E major above moving second viola and first cello.
The sextet returns to the walking music after the woman’s confession.
The upper strings withdraw over E♭ minor, leaving a low B♭ in the second cello.

composer.epithet: He removed the home key from music, kept learning from Bach and Brahms, and found room for a minuet among all twelve notes.
facts: Largely self-taught; lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky
Alban Berg and Anton Webern from 1904; later Hanns Eisler and John Cage
Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33; UCLA, 1936–44
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
At the première of Pierrot lunaire in Berlin on 16 October 1912, Albertine Zehme stood onstage in a Pierrot costume. Behind a screen, five instrumentalists watched Arnold Schoenberg conduct. They had held twenty-five ensemble rehearsals to prepare thirty-odd minutes of music in which the voice slid away from its written notes, a flute could turn into a piccolo, and a violinist had to pick up a viola. The screen concealed one of the busiest small orchestras ever assembled.

Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt in 1874 and began learning the violin as a child. His father died when he was fifteen. From 1891 to 1895 he worked in a bank, making music with friends and teaching himself from scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him lessons. Brahms showed him how a small phrase could grow by changing; Wagner showed him how long a chord could keep us waiting.
